f65c04e6cdbeb9af: JOHOR BARU: Ten vehicles caught fire at the underground car park of a shopping centre in Jalan Wong Ah Fook.
Videos showing thick black smoke emerging from the underground level were shared on social media.
Three women suffered breathing difficulties in the incident.
Operation commander Senior Fire Officer 1 Suffian Sulaiman said the women received initial treatment from firefighters before a 48-year-old woman was taken to hospital.
The women, aged 48, 35 and 57, included a Singaporean, he said in a statement today.
Suffian said firefighters received a call about the incident at 3.40pm, with a fire engine from Larkin Fire and Rescue Station arriving about six minutes later.
The operation involved personnel and fire engines from the Larkin, Tebrau and Kempas fire and rescue stations, as well as the Mount Austin Volunteer Fire Brigade, with a total of 40 personnel.
The fire involved vehicles on the second basement level of the shopping centre.
Eight vehicles were 80 to 90 per cent burnt, while the other two were 20 to 30 per cent burnt, Suffian said.
Firefighters used two streams, each 91m long, from the building's fire protection system and fire engine pumps.
An inspection found that the fire protection system and exhaust fans at the site were not functioning.
Firefighters also checked the area to ensure no other victims were trapped.
The firefighting and inspection operations were still ongoing.
9bf7d24df995b800: PETALING JAYA: Police investigations on Jempol MP Shamsulkahar Deli over remarks he made while campaigning in the Negeri Sembilan election are still continuing as the probe papers have been returned to the police by the state prosecutor’s office.

In a written parliamentary reply, home minister Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the initial stage of the investigation had been completed and the probe papers referred to the Negeri Sembilan prosecutor’s office on Aug 21 for review and further instructions.
He said the probe papers were returned on Sept 3 with further instructions for the investigating officer.
“Accordingly, the investigation is still ongoing, after which the investigation paper will be resubmitted to the state prosecutor’s office for further instructions."
On July 29, Negeri Sembilan police chief Alzafny Ahmad said police had received a report from a 55-year-old complainant who saw a video clip of Shamsulkahar’s speech during a ceramah.

The MP is being investigated for allegedly making statements intended to cause public fear or alarm, the improper use of network services, and promoting ill will and hostility during the election campaign.

Several DAP leaders, including Jelutong MP RSN Rayer, had also lodged a police report against Shamsulkahar over his remarks allegedly linking the party to an image deemed insulting to the Sultan of Selangor.

Rayer said the Umno MP allegedly referred to the edited image of a pig in royal attire, which is believed to have targeted Selangor ruler Sultan Sharafuddin Idris Shah, before asking why DAP had dared to do such a thing.
He said Shamsulkahar’s remarks gave the audience the false impression that DAP was responsible for producing the image.
Rayer accused Shamsulkahar of making defamatory and malicious remarks against the party and urged the police to conduct a thorough investigation.
b2e340e94d563847: PETALING JAYA: Kementerian Perpaduan Negara membuat keputusan untuk tidak meneruskan penubuhan Suruhanjaya Keharmonian Negara (SKN), selepas membangkitkan semula cadangan itu pada April.

Menteri Aaron Ago Dagang berkata, keputusan dibuat selepas dua sesi libat urus melibatkan kumpulan masyarakat sivil, agensi kerajaan, pakar akademik, pemimpin masyarakat dan pihak berkepentingan lain bagi menilai keperluan, skop, implikasi, cabaran dan kebolehlaksanaan.

"Selepas mengambil kira pandangan semua pihak serta penelitian lanjut Kementerian, KPN memutuskan untuk tidak meneruskan penubuhan SKN sebagai entiti baharu," menurut jawapan bertulis di laman Parlimen.

Katanya, kementerian akan memberi tumpuan kepada pengukuhan institusi sedia ada, iaitu Jabatan Perpaduan Negara dan Integrasi Nasional (JPNIN), Komuniti Rukun Tetangga dan Mediator Komuniti, yang dilihat sebagai pendekatan yang praktikal, responsif dan kos efektif untuk memperkukuh pengurusan keharmonian sosial.
"Di samping itu, cadangan ini juga dapat mengelakkan pertindihan fungsi dan kos penubuhan entiti baharu, di samping memanfaatkan struktur, jaringan dan instrumen sedia ada.
Majlis Konsultasi Perpaduan Negara menyediakan tiga draf Rang Undang-undang (RUU) termasuk RUU Suruhanjaya Keharmonian dan Rekonsiliasi Nasional (SKRN), pada 2015.

Cadangan penubuhan SKRN pula telah dipersetujui pada dasarnya, namun pelaksanaannya tertangguh berikutan pertindihan bidang kuasa dengan agensi sedia ada seperti Suruhanjaya Hak Asasi Manusia Malaysia dan polis.
Pada April 2020, kerajaan memutuskan agar cadangan tersebut tidak diteruskan.

Pada April tahun ini, Aaron mengumumkan JPNIN akan mengerakkan semula usaha ke arah menggubal RUU SKRN, dengan penekanan kepada pendekatan pencegahan dan pendamaian, selepas mengambil kira peningkatan polemik berkaitan perpaduan yang menggugat keharmonian masyarakat.
098e12ba9e746fe8: MIDDLE East crude exports recently climbed to their highest levels since the start of the Iran war as more Gulf producers resume transit through the Strait of Hormuz —despite the continued threat of Iranian attacks. Yet oil prices remain stubbornly elevated, suggesting logistical problems are proving as disruptive as outright supply losses.

Crude flows through the embattled waterway reached 14.2 million barrels per day on a seven-day average on Sept 26, nearly 80 per cent of pre-war levels. While volumes have declined since, they will likely be revised higher because ships often disable satellite tracking systems while traversing the strait and for several days thereafter.
Either way, the trend is clear: a lot more crude is getting through the strait. So why is Brent still trading above US$100 per barrel? In a word, logistics.

For decades, the global oil industry functioned as a finely tuned system designed to move enormous volumes of crude and fuels over long distances at the lowest possible cost. The conflicts in the Middle East and Eastern Europe have fractured that model, as a combination of record-high tanker rates, soaring insurance costs and a severe shortage of refining capacity has created bottlenecks across the energy supply chain.
Those problems may take months, if not years, to unwind, leaving consumers facing persistently high energy bills—even if the crude supply squeeze continues to ease.

Iran's blockade of Hormuz following the onset of the war with the United States and Israel on Feb 28 rapidly reshaped global oil flows. Gulf producers diverted supplies through alternative routes, buyers sought barrels from more distant regions and governments released unprecedented volumes of oil from strategic reserves.

One of the biggest changes was that Saudi Arabia — previously the world's largest oil exporter — diverted its exports through its East-West pipeline, which delivers crude to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. At one point this year, four per cent of global oil supplies were via this route.

However, after the pipeline came under attack by Iranian-backed Iraqi militias in early last month, Saudi Arabia was forced to redirect exports back to the Gulf via Hormuz, which it discovered, could be more easily transited than previously thought.
Saudi exports through Hormuz averaged three million bpd last month, the highest level during the conflict, according to Kpler.

While Saudi Arabia's crude exports through Hormuz last month were still only around half of pre-war volumes, the kingdom's exports could quickly near pre-war levels as the East-West pipeline gradually returns to normal operations.

Ironically, then, the attack on the East-West pipeline, which was intended to cripple Riyadh, may have instead weakened Teheran's most powerful leverage—its purported control of the strait — by demonstrating that large volumes can still transit Hormuz and other major export hubs despite continued attacks.
Yet the recovery remains fragile.
But geopolitics is only part of the story.
Freight and insurance costs, once a relatively minor component of the delivered price of oil, have become major price drivers, partly due to the current shuttle system operating around the Gulf.
At the same time, buyers are increasingly sourcing crude from the Atlantic Basin and shipping it to Asia over longer routes, further tightening tanker supply.
The result has been a surge in key tanker rates to record highs. Freight costs that once accounted for around three per cent of the delivered price of a barrel now represent roughly 27 per cent.
These costs are unlikely to normalise until trade flows return to something resembling their prewar pattern.
The loss of refining capacity in the Middle East and Russia, where Ukrainian drone attacks have crippled dozens of plants, has compounded the problem, particularly for diesel.
The Group of Seven's decision last week to release diesel from strategic stocks will likely provide only temporary relief as it does nothing to restore lost refining capacity.

What's more, refiners are increasingly competing for the medium-sour crude grades that generate higher diesel yields. Those barrels are concentrated in the Middle East and Russia, precisely the regions where supply disruptions remain most severe.
The result is that oil prices are no longer primarily a function of supply, but of the industry's ability to transport and process crude —making it much more challenging to bring these prices down.
The writer is from Reuters

299c4586da0ccf13: Microsoft is adding two extra file types to its Outlook block list to strengthen security. The file types are .msix and .msixbundle, used for Windows application packages and bundles. The change affects New Outlook for Windows and Outlook on the Web in Exchange Online. By default, users of the affected clients will no longer be able to download or open attachments with these extensions, which is no bad thing because blindly installing a malicious .msix package could compromise a device. That said, although Microsoft noted that the file types were "infrequently used," there are legitimate reasons for their presence in emails. Administrators who need to permit these attachments can add the extensions to the AllowedFileTypes property of the relevant OwaMailboxPolicy before the rollout, scheduled for early to mid-November 2026. "This update is part of our ongoing efforts to strengthen security and help protect organizations from potentially unsafe file attachments," Microsoft said. The Windows giant's application packaging system has come under fire over the years. Microsoft disabled the ms-appinstaller protocol handler by default in December 2023 after attackers abused it to distribute malware. The attachment block adds another layer of protection, unless administrators explicitly allow these file types. Other file types blocked by Outlook on the Web include .py Python files, .ps1 PowerShell files, and .cab files. It's a little surprising that it has taken until now for .msix and .msixbundle to be added to the list, considering the havoc malicious packages can wreak on a system. Renaming an attachment's extension or sending a download link may get around the attachment restriction, but neither makes the package safe. Persuading someone to download and install it remains a route for miscreants, even with Windows' other protections in place. ®

ff291680e81eaa4f: PETALING JAYA: There are around 40.77 million registered vehicles in Malaysia, of which 26.6 million or about 65.3% are active, says transport minister Loke Siew Fook.
In a written parliamentary reply, Loke said this was about a two million increase compared with the 38.7 million vehicles registered at the end of 2024.
He said some 1.62 million new vehicles were registered in 2025, including 847,000 cars and 703,000 motorcycles.
"Of the 26.6 million active vehicles, nearly 16 million are cars and 9.57 million are motorcycles," he said when replying to a question from Zahari Kechik (PN-Jeli).
Loke said the growth in the number of personal vehicles had contributed to worsening traffic congestion, with productivity decreasing due to Malaysians spending more time in traffic.
"This continuous dependence on personal vehicles also incurs higher transport costs and contributes to air pollution, while burdening road infrastructure."
Loke said his ministry had launched multiple initiatives to boost public transport use and reduce dependence on personal vehicles, including the new LRT3 and Mutiara LRT lines.
f6667befc2d65554: STRASBOURG: The European Commission on Tuesday proposed limiting Ukraine's access to farm subsidies if it joins the EU and tightening "safeguards" on all newcomers, as Brussels grapples with how to keep the bloc workable should it expand.
Russia's 2022 invasion of its neighbour breathed fresh impetus into efforts to expand the EU as Ukraine and Moldova joined the queue of countries seeking membership.
The ex-Soviet duo are now among four frontrunners, with Montenegro pressing to become the EU's 28th member next year and Albania not too far behind.

But while Brussels insists enlargement is a strategic priority, there are major fears that adding new members – especially war-torn giant Ukraine – could shred the EU's budget and render the bloc unmanageable.
In a bid to alleviate the worries of its current members, the EU's executive set out a series of "safeguards" to make sure newcomers don't backslide on democracy or hoover up too many key resources.
"So the main question has been: Is the EU fit for another enlargement? And there is a clear yes, a future enlargement is possible," said EU commissioner Marta Kos.
"But at the same time, there are some risks, and we have identified areas where we will need adjustments."

The prospect of agricultural powerhouse Ukraine joining one day has sparked fears in countries such as France and Poland that it would sap the EU's vast programme of farm subsidies and flood the market with cheaper produce.
Kos said Brussels was proposing "special arrangements which would limit the financial support" and restrictions on exports of some products from Ukraine such as wheat.
More broadly, Brussels is also seeking to learn from the bitter experience of Hungary's repeated blockages under former leader Viktor Orban by trying to make sure newcomers can't cause such trouble.
It wants to introduce new "safeguards" for 15 years after countries join against blocking the EU's functioning or rolling back the rule of law and make it easier to punish them if they do.
"No more Viktor Orbans," said Kos.
Meanwhile, Brussels also said it wants to get new countries to commit to not block others from joining.

While most of the changes would only apply to new entrants starting with Montenegro, the commission said that current members should also switch from needing unanimity to majority approval in areas such as foreign policy.
That would limit the chances of countries using their vetoes to bung up the system, but it seems unlikely to fly, as numerous member states are loath to give up a key power.
'Roadmaps' to membership
EU leaders will debate the proposals at a summit next week, and officials are hoping they at least give a clear signal they are still open for enlargement.
Tuesday's proposal had been delayed for months as various EU countries have pushed a variety of ideas.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz earlier this year floated giving countries an "associate membership" status before fully joining that could allow them to attend – but not vote – at EU meetings.
That plan received short shrift from a raft of EU countries and Ukraine, who saw it as a way of trapping wannabe members in a permanent halfway house.
There has also been pushback against any idea of speeding up the process.
In a bid to offset any complaints by the candidates, Brussels has said it will soon lay out "roadmaps" for the four frontrunners to try to pin down their path towards membership.
The commission is also pushing for the "gradual integration" of would-be members to align them closer with the bloc's single market before joining.
While the EU debates the future shape of the union, the four frontrunners look set to take further steps towards joining next week.
But while Ukraine should open two new areas of negotiations, there is still a long road of arduous reforms ahead for the country, and it could be many years before it becomes a member.

9250628ed307c75d: Lately, questions have been raised over how private firms entrusted with collecting public funds handle government money.

The concerns warrant a closer examination of the safeguards governing contractor arrangements, particularly when large sums are outside direct government control. Two recent cases —involving Zetrix AI Bhd and Dapat Vista Sdn Bhd —highlight starkly different concerns — ranging from delayed remittance of collected funds to placing public money into commercial interest-bearing accounts.
Zetrix AI, acting on behalf of the Road Transport Department, collected RM314 million in various fees but failed to remit the funds.
Meanwhile, Dapat Vista, the operator of court bail payment system e-Jamin, collected RM193.71 million in deposits as at 2024 without a formal contract with the government.

Neither case should be viewed in isolation. Findings by the auditor general and the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) on weaknesses in government oversight point to vulnerabilities in the systems governing outsourced collection and management of public funds.
The issue is not simply whether any individual contractor breached its obligations, but whether the government's checks-and-balances were robust enough to prevent these failures.

The issues highlighted deep-seated structural and administrative vulnerabilities. Still, it's too much of a coincidence and it should compel enforcement authorities to examine every ministry, department and agency dealing with external billing contractors.
The Auditor General's Report 2/2026 revealed that the government failed to recover RM68.81 million in advance payments across 24 projects.

Almost 87 per cent of the debt remained uncollected for over 10 years. What went wrong? These ministries failed to pursue legal claims against errant contractors, many of whom conveniently went bankrupt or were dissolved.
They were also slow in filing "proof of debt" claims, leaving the government as an unprotected and unsecured creditor.

How was this permitted? The issue stems from special administrative exemptions granted to departments — exemptions that inexplicably continued even after contractors failed to meet standard Treasury controls meant to prevent operational bottlenecks.

However, there is now a legal tool to stop these abuses: the Government Procurement Act 2025 which introduces personal liability and strict penalties for unauthorised interference in public fund management.
The catch: the Act is enforceable only in 2027 so as to give ministries and private contractors a grace period.
The PAC recommended that the judiciary develop a proprietary system to eliminate vendor dependency and ensure full data ownership.
This sound advice should be extended across all arms of government, especially agencies that sub-contract critical functions or the collection of public funds
e81043418dfeb9c4: MIT is launching a new strategic initiative today: MIT for America, which seeks to strengthen STEM education nationally, at many levels of learning.  Addressing a critical national need, the initiative ranges across STEM fields and will engage students from kindergarten through community college, preparing them to live and work in a world increasingly shaped by science and technology. MIT for America’s programs will develop new opportunities for student achievement in mathematics, hands-on design and fabrication, and constructive engagement with artificial intelligence.  President Sally Kornbluth made the announcement today in a letter to the Institute community. “A natural extension of the Institute’s long record of national service, MIT for America is grounded in our deep belief in potential over pedigree, of the transformative power of learning by doing and in the open sharing of knowledge,” Kornbluth wrote. The initiative represents an Institute-wide effort to address the national challenge of improving STEM education and helping it adapt to shifting societal needs. MIT for America will leverage the Institute’s longstanding strengths to develop new programs and expand existing projects, while amplifying MIT’s impact on national education. MIT for America’s faculty leaders emphasize that the initiative will support programs that can be scaled up and that provide direct, face-to-face guidance for learners and educators.  “The goal is to provide programs that are both scalable and high-touch, and make an impact across the country,” says Professor Eric Klopfer, a faculty co-director of MIT for America and director of the Scheller Teacher Education Program and the Education Arcade at MIT. “All our programs take advantage of things we are well-positioned to do at MIT, and can be distributed around the country. That’s our guiding light.”  Cynthia Breazeal, faculty co-director of MIT for America, professor of media arts and sciences, and the Benesse Professor of Research in Education, says the initiative “is about bringing high-quality access to STEM and AI education, from kindergarten to community college, across the United States. We live in an innovation-driven world, and it’s important to have an education that gives you access to it, whether that’s so you can be a fully engaged citizen or have the opportunity for economic mobility.” Breazeal adds: “Talent is everywhere. We think opportunity should be, too.”  The initiative is addressing large-scale needs in STEM education. Only 29 percent of U.S. students in grades 9-12 build circuits, and only 6 percent of students enroll in computer science classes, even though about 60 percent of high schools offer such courses. MIT for America intends to substantially help communities across the country build the bandwidth needed to further develop STEM knowledge and workplace skills.  “This effort is about really rolling up sleeves and getting out there and engaging communities, and helping to build capacity across the United States,” Breazeal adds. MIT for America features programs addressing three high-priority areas: Mathematical thinking and problem solving: Work here builds on an existing program, the MIT for America Calculus Project, launched a year ago, in which MIT students and alumni volunteer to help provide calculus tutoring to students in school districts across the country.  Living, learning, and working with AI: This area addresses multiple issues revolving around AI, including teacher education that helps instructors integrate AI into classroom learning in productive ways, and programs that enhance AI skills and STEM education in technical-vocational schools and community colleges. The MIT RAISE program (Responsible AI for Social Empowerment and Education) is a leader in this domain.  Designing, making, and innovating: MIT for America plans to build out programs that encourage hands-on learning, design work, use of fab labs and makerspaces, and experiential learning, sometimes deploying tools such as national design challenges.  “Across the U.S., we want to unlock opportunities and experiences where students are,” says Claudia Urrea, head of MIT for America and head of the MIT pK-12 Initiative. “We want to find people who have not had the opportunity to discover their talent.” In the first case, the MIT for America Calculus Project provides a ready model of outreach with growth potential. About half of U.S. school districts offer calculus, but many of those districts may be under-resourced. The MIT for America Calculus Project has been growing in partnership with an increasing number of school districts, while MIT undergraduates and alumni have enjoyed participating in the program.   “People have been really excited about the MIT for America Calculus Project, seeing both the impact that it has, and its model, which I think has resonated,” Klopfer says. “That’s really representative of what other programs could look like.” In the second topic area, MIT for America can leverage burgeoning efforts such as MIT RAISE. The program helps educate teachers and engage students about implementing AI in ways that can complement the developing skills of students, enabling them to use AI in productive ways. “RAISE is about providing materials and training for teachers that helps them have conversations and productive activities around AI,” Klopfer says. “It’s about understanding how AI works and discussing what the values are in your school. It has to be active, involving the students. If you try to force things, about AI one way or the other, that will fail.” In an outgrowth of RAISE, MIT also launched a related program, Pathways for AI Training and Hiring (PATH), on Oct. 1. Starting with a partnership with Georgia State University, PATH aims to bring AI training to two-year and four-year colleges, to help students gain AI skills useful for workplaces.  “RAISE has had a lot of success with scaling already,” Breazeal says, noting that about 1 million students were involved with RAISE’s Day of AI event earlier this year. “At MIT, we want to empower youth voices to shape the future. It’s an excellent example of our ability to do that.” And in the third topic area, MIT for America can help produce substantial growth in programs aimed at hands-on learning. That may include more projects such as MIT’s Regenerative Futures Challenge, a global program stemming from MIT’s pK-12 Initiative, which give students the opportunity to create climate and sustainability solutions. Additionally, the Fab Foundation, which grew out of MIT’s Center for Bits and Atoms Fab Lab program, offers tools and curriculum to learners at 300 fab labs across the U.S. “It’s about coming together in places where there are people who can work together, mentor each other, and learn by example,” Klopfer says. “That’s the kind of thing we want to be creating at scale. We want to build on that.” All told, MIT for America represents a vigorous all-campus effort to enhance education through sustained outreach and knowledge-sharing. At MIT, partners in creating the initiative include the MIT Media Lab; MIT RAISE; the MIT pK-12 Initiative; the Office of the Vice President for Resource Development; and the Office of Innovation and Strategy. The leaders of MIT for America presented an overview of the program in September at MIT’s Alumni Leadership Conference, and they say alumni activity around the new initiative will be another key to its success.  “We really appreciate the support and engagement of our alumni,” Breazeal says. “We know they care about K-12 education and access to community colleges.” More broadly, she adds, “We do think this message will resonate with people all across the country.” “I look forward to watching these programs flourish, evolve, and grow,” Kornbluth wrote to the community.

1c8bd6a534dfb432: KUALA LUMPUR: Muslims must master technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) without losing their values, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said.
"Do not, in craving change and new knowledge, abandon our principles of faith, morals and character and be sidelined from the mainstream as good Muslims," he said.
Anwar said mastering AI was a must for the ummah.
"Must we master it? My answer is that it is a must. An ummah that abandons AI as new knowledge will be left behind," he said.
He said Malaysia's understanding of AI need not be copied wholesale from other countries, particularly the West.
Anwar was speaking at the opening of the 66th International Al-Quran Recitation and Memorisation Assembly (MTHQA) at the World Trade Centre Kuala Lumpur here.

Also present were Minister in the Prime Minister's Department (Religious Affairs) Dr Zulkifli Hasan, Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil and Chief Secretary to the Government Tan Sri Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar.
Anwar said the discussion on AI could be viewed through a question posed to the Islamic world nearly a century ago.
In 1929, scholar Sheikh Muhammad Basiuni Imran from Sambas wrote to Cairo journal Al-Manar asking why Muslims were backward when they represented the true religion, while the West was advancing.
The question was passed to Lebanese thinker Amir Shakib Arslan, whose answer was published in 1930.

Anwar said Arslan replied that Muslims accepted the religion but did not live by it, while others practised traits it taught, such as discipline, order, governance and cleanliness, and reaped the benefits.
"If young people asked that question today, it would still be relevant," he said.

Anwar said a mighty ummah required faith, knowledge, morals, character-building, the spirit of struggle and the courage to bring change, grounded in returning to the study, understanding and practice of the Quran.

He said several well-known ulama who recently visited Malaysia had urged a return to "turath", the Islamic intellectual legacy of more than 1,400 years, and that it should not be set aside because of new figures who claimed to master all knowledge.

The 66th MTHQA, held from Oct 6 to 10, carries the theme "Madani Dihayati, Ummah Diberkati" and brings together 50 participants from 38 countries, comprising 25 in the recitation (tilawah) category and 25 in the memorisation (hafazan) category.

Malaysia is represented by Mohamad Cik Hasnul Taqiyuddin Cik Sazali and Nur Syakura Mohamad Musa in the tilawah category, and Muhammad Izzul Afnan Sazali and Dina Hadfina Mohd Umarul Hisyam in the hafazan category.
18d1e91cd7eb5dcb: PETALING JAYA: The national unity ministry has decided not to proceed with setting up a national harmony commission, after reviving the proposal in April.

National unity minister Aaron Ago Dagang said this decision was made after conducting two engagement sessions with civil society groups, government agencies, academics, community leaders and other stakeholders on the proposed commission's scope, implications, challenges and feasibility.
"After considering the views of all parties, the ministry decided not to proceed with establishing a national harmony commission as a new entity.
"The ministry will focus on strengthening existing institutions, namely the national unity and integration department, the respective Rukun Tetangga, and community mediators.

"These institutions will serve as agents to manage social harmony, as part of a practical, responsive and cost-effective approach to strengthen the management of social harmony," he said in a written parliamentary reply.
Aaron added that a commission would have overlapping functions with the existing institutions and lead to unnecessary additional costs.
The national unity consultation council had prepared three draft bills in 2015, including the national harmony and reconciliation commission bill.

Aaron previously said the government agreed in principle on the national harmony and reconciliation commission bill in 2019, though its implementation was delayed due to overlaps in jurisdiction with the police and Suhakam.

In April 2020, the Perikatan Nasional-led government decided not to proceed with the bill, but Aaron's ministry revived the proposal in April this year, citing a "rise in unity-related polemics that threaten national harmony".

The seized items were taken to the Hilir Perak district police headquarters. The case is being investigated under Section 135(1)(d) of the Customs Act 1967.
Chua said investigations were ongoing to identify the source of the cigarettes, those involved and the distribution network.
Those convicted can be fined at least 10 times the amount of customs duty or RM100,000, whichever is higher.
The maximum penalty is a fine of up to 20 times the amount of customs duty or RM500,000, whichever is higher, or imprisonment of between six months and five years, or both.
Chua urged the public not to become involved in possessing, storing, selling or distributing untaxed goods, or acting as intermediaries.
He said Hilir Perak police would continue operations, intelligence gathering and enforcement action to curb the smuggling and distribution of contraband in the district.

ae343c23f74ed22a: BEIJING: China called on France and Germany to steer clear of "protectionist" trade measures on Tuesday, after their leaders urged the EU to develop a legal arsenal for a potential trade war.

French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen that "we need a credible instrument" for swift and decisive action.
This includes the ability to cut off access to the European single market "if needed", according to the letter seen by AFP on Monday.
Macron and Merz stopped short of explicitly naming China, but their letter comes just days before EU trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic heads to Beijing to tackle trade frictions.
China's commerce ministry, in a statement on Tuesday, urged France and Germany to "refrain from encouraging the EU to resort to protectionist tools at every turn".
"We hope that France and Germany, as major economies in the world, will uphold openness, cooperation and free trade," the ministry said in a statement.
"They should avoid going down the wrong path in the wrong way, only to ultimately suffer the consequences themselves."

Berlin and Paris want to give the European Commission the power to respond to a trade aggression within days. Under their proposal, such action would not need approval from the EU's 27 countries, though a weighted majority of states could block it.
The EU's biggest trade concern is its deficit with China, which Brussels says is inflicting damage on key European sectors.
Beijing's foreign ministry, also responding to the leaders' letter on Tuesday, called the economic and trade relationship between China and the EU "mutually beneficial".

"We hope the EU will work with China in the same direction, address each other's concerns through dialogue and consultation, and jointly maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains," ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said in a statement.

6a32b84d42dbc994: BEIJING: Novak Djokovic won the China Open on Tuesday after his opponent Alex de Minaur retired from the final, extending an astonishing unbeaten streak in Beijing and winning the 102nd title of his career.
The 39-year-old Serbian won the first set in the tie-break 7-6 (7/3) and was down a game in the second set when the Australian ended the match early.
"I always want to visualise myself with the trophy, particularly here in Beijing," Djokovic said during the trophy ceremony.
"But I was also quite aware that reality is a little bit different these days," he said, adding that it had been a challenging year with "physical and health issues".
"I was just trying to find the good feeling on the court," he said.
The first set was a physical battle that lasted more than one hour, and both men needed medical timeouts before the second.
De Minaur, the world number nine, won the first game of the second set before retiring.
It was not immediately clear why de Minaur left the match, but he walked back onto the court after his medical timeout with a white wrap around his left thigh.
"I don't feel great," de Minaur told the crowd afterwards.
"I want to say sorry to the amazing fans that came to watch... I didn't want to finish like this," the 27-year-old added.

De Minaur advanced to the final after his opponent Hubert Hurkacz retired injured from their semi-final on Monday, while Djokovic moved through when Daniil Medvedev was disqualified for hitting a fan with a ball.
With the win, Djokovic extended a perfect record to 34 wins in as many matches for his seventh title in the Chinese capital – his first since 2015.
He put on a valiant show to lift the trophy, ousting top seed Alexander Zverev in the quarter-final and coming back to defeat home hopeful Bu Yunchaokete in a demanding three sets.
Djokovic, a 24-time Grand Slam champion, will finish the season with a title for the 21st consecutive year.
'Really grateful'
In the women's draw, Karolina Muchova beat former world number one Naomi Osaka on her ninth match point to reach the quarter-finals, triumphant in a tense tie-break.
Muchova, the seventh seed, overcame 50 unforced errors across the two-hour-and-52-minute match to beat Osaka 7-5, 1-6, 7-6 (9/7).
Osaka, who represents Japan, saved eight match points but could not get past Muchova's match-winning volley.
"I was shaking. I'm happy I made the last volley... Naomi could be standing here. It's me, and I'm really grateful for it," the 30-year-old Czech player told the crowd.
She next faces compatriot Nikola Bartunkova.
Earlier, Russia's Mirra Andreeva beat Ukraine's Daria Snigur 6-2, 6-2 to book her quarter-final spot against fellow Russian Ekaterina Alexandrova.
Alexandrova, ranked 28th, upset Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova 6-2, 6-2, ending the Czech player's bid to return to the Beijing final that she reached last year.

862c910810bf20d8: Microsoft is very keen for Outlook users to ditch the classic version in favor of the new one, and a search bug isn't helping the old client's cause. Users will still be able to switch back to Classic Outlook. The next stage, cutover, will remove the option to change back. Microsoft has, however, still managed to find time to load Classic Outlook with Copilot via a button beside the ribbon, along with the odd bug or two, like the borking of the Quick Steps function. Microsoft also acknowledged an issue that prevented some users from accessing voicemail audio attachments. The voicemail issue was fixed in build 16.0.20430.2000 and later, but the Server Assisted Search problem remains. Another update for Outlook on the Web and New Outlook to make the new tools look a bit like Classic Outlook began rolling out recently. Something to ease the transition. However, it's only skin deep. 2841bd8626195c8f: NEW YORK: Targeted financial support, rather than broad subsidies, is the most effective way to protect vulnerable households when inflation surges, says the International Monetary Fund (IMF).

In its global economic outlook for October titled "Navigating a Shock-Prone World: Lessons from Cost-of-Living Crises," the IMF said targeted and temporary cash transfers can cushion poorer households against price spikes for essentials while limiting the burden on public finances.
It said such assistance directs limited resources to those most in need while allowing higher market prices to signal scarcity and incentivise consumers to reduce consumption, Xinhua reported.
The IMF said support should be calibrated to the temporary portion of a price shock and include clear expiration dates, rather than compensate households for permanently higher prices.
If governments broaden eligibility, assistance should remain tied to the average impact of the shock on lower-income households, it added.

Its recommendations come after prices for everyday essentials, including food, electricity and fuel, rose sharply in many countries, putting pressure on household budgets and, in some cases, threatening broader economic stability.
The IMF said the effects can persist long after the initial surge in food and energy prices fades.
Inflation expectations can remain above pre-crisis levels for years, while falling real wages erode households’ purchasing power.
With economies increasingly exposed to shocks, governments should strengthen social protection systems before crises hit, the IMF said.
Doing so could make future interventions more effective while preserving fiscal space to respond to new shocks, it added.

He said decisions should not be made on impulse or without considering their consequences.

"You cannot be taking decisions on an impulse. You can't be doing it without thinking through the processes," he said at the Khazanah Megatrends Forum at the Mandarin Oriental Kuala Lumpur here today.
Khazanah Nasional Bhd managing director Datuk Amirul Feisal Wan Zahir, Deputy Finance Minister Liew Chin Tong and Khazanah Research Institute chairman Dr Nungsari Ahmad Radhi were also present.
Amir Hamzah said government decisions had widespread and lasting effects, making it important to consider how they could change people's lives.
He said the Fiscal Responsibility Act provided safeguards for managing public finances.
"Bringing down fiscal deficits to below a certain level is important to make sure the fiscal position of the government is strong enough to ride and grow the country going forward.
"Because what we don't want to do is borrow from our children and our grandchildren," he said.
Amir Hamzah said wealth generated from depleting resources, including oil and gas, must also be preserved so future generations could benefit.
He said the funds could be used in areas including education, skills development and health.
He said the broader aim was to improve people's lives.
"Maybe not for us, maybe for our children, maybe for our grandchildren," he added.

addcfa4e123a108a: SINGAPORE: Singapore’s state court on Tuesday fined two men S$3.35 million (about RM10.7 million) each for importing more than 4.5 million litres of diesel from Malaysia without the required declarations, thereby evading customs duty and goods and services tax (GST).
Singapore customs said the two Singaporeans, Chua E Hong, 51, and Ng Leok Kwee, 48, pleaded guilty to three charges of fraudulent evasion of duty under the Customs Act.
The charges involved the importation of 4,527,099 litres of automotive diesel oil between April and December 2024, with about S$905,419 in duty evaded.
The court also took into consideration 16 other charges during the two men’s sentencing, comprising six charges for fraudulent evasion of duty and 10 charges of fraudulent evasion of GST.
The total duty and GST evaded by the two men amounted to about S$2,500,205, Singapore Customs said in a statement on Tuesday.
According to customs, the pair devised a scheme to source cheaper diesel from Malaysia and import it into Singapore without declaring the imports or obtaining the required cargo clearance permits.
It said the diesel was subsequently sold to customers in Singapore to increase the profits of CNC Petroleum Pte Ltd, of which Chua was the managing director and Ng was the executive director.
“Acting on information received, Singapore customs investigated and uncovered the scheme to import diesel into Singapore without the required declarations and permits.
“Under the scheme, CNC purchased the diesel from suppliers' terminals in Pengerang, Johor,” it said.

Singapore customs said a vessel collected the diesel and transported it into Singapore’s territorial waters, where it was transferred at Selat Pauh Petroleum Anchorage to two smaller vessels on multiple occasions.
“The diesel was subsequently transported to Penjuru Terminal and transferred to tanker trucks for distribution to customers in Singapore.
“Ng coordinated the scheduling of the vessels and tanker trucks, as well as the collection and transfer of the diesel,” it said.

d88c1f95baf91f31: TANJONG MALIM, Oct 6 — Time may have passed, but the image of the late former Perak police chief Tan Sri Khoo Chong Kong as a loving father and a firm, courageous police officer remains vivid for his daughter, Datin Rita Koo Swee Kim.

Rita, 78, said a pantomime performance held in conjunction with the official opening of the Muallim District Police Headquarters (IPD) today rekindled memories of her father, nearly 51 years after his death, leaving her deeply moved.

“I was 25 at the time and living in Seremban (Negeri Sembilan) after getting married. I received a call from a police officer telling me that something had happened to my father, but I was given no further details.

“When we heard the news, my husband and I rushed back to Ipoh to see my father and find out what had happened to him. He had been attacked with a weapon. I’m really touched that the Royal Malaysia Police, especially the Perak police, still remember him after all these years,” she said when met here today.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Datin Rita Koo Swee Kim (second left), daughter of the late former Perak police chief Tan Sri Koo Chong Kong, poses with her husband and child beside the original uniform worn by Koo when he was shot dead by communist elements on November 13, 1975, at an exhibition in Ipoh on October 6, 2026. — Bernama pic
Earlier, the Sultan of Perak Sultan Nazrin Shah officiated the opening of the Muallim IPD.

Rita, Khoo’s eldest daughter, said one of the memories closest to her heart was how devoted her father was to his work, often spending long hours on duty, particularly during his service with the Special Branch and operations to combat communist activities.
She said there were times when her father had to be away from home for one or two months to carry out operations, leaving her mother worried about his safety.
“He was always very busy. There were times when he would leave for an operation and be gone for one or two months. We never knew exactly when he would be coming home,” she said.
Rita said that despite his firm and serious demeanour while on duty, her father was a loving and caring man at home.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Datin Rita Koo Swee Kim, daughter of the late former Perak police chief Tan Sri Koo Chong Kong, speaks during an interview at an exhibition held in conjunction with the opening of the Muallim District Police Headquarters in Ipoh on October 6, 2026. — Bernama pic

She also described him as a man who stood firmly by his principles and would not compromise on what he believed was right, saying his courage in carrying out his duties had always been an inspiration to her.

Meanwhile, Rita said seeing the official car her father once used and the blood-stained uniform he wore during the incident was an emotional experience, bringing back memories of her father and the sacrifice he made in the line of duty.

“It really takes me back to those days. I had seen the car at a museum before, but seeing it again today, together with his uniform and hearing the stories about him, really brought back so many memories,” she said.

Born on November 12, 1925, in Kwangsi, China, the late Khoo was raised in Ipoh and joined the Sarawak Constabulary as an inspector on November 5, 1952, before holding several key positions and eventually becoming Perak police chief on January 7, 1975.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Beside the official car once used by her late father, former Perak police chief Tan Sri Koo Chong Kong, Datin Rita Koo Swee Kim (right) poses with her child at an exhibition in Ipoh on October 6, 2026. Koo was shot dead by communist elements on November 13, 1975. — Bernama pic

He was shot while travelling home from the Perak Police Contingent Headquarters to his residence on Jalan Tawar, Ipoh, at about 1pm on November 13, 1975, in an attack believed to have been carried out by communist insurgents.
His driver, Corporal Yeong Peng Cheong, was also killed in the attack, while Khoo succumbed to his injuries on November 14, 1975, about 28 hours after he was shot. — Bernama
* Editor’s note: IPD is the abbreviation in Malay for Ibu Pejabat Polis Daerah (District Police Headquarters).
aa8e9c9b63b38edd: NAHARIYA (Israel), Oct 6 — On Israel’s border with Lebanon, where Hezbollah fired thousands of rockets and drones, previous backers of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu say they are rethinking how they will vote in the first election since the war.
“Many I know were right-wing and were Bibi supporters, and today they’re not,” said plant nursery owner Sigal Malachi, using a nickname for Israel’s longest-serving premier.

In traditional strongholds of Netanyahu support, many told AFP they could no longer back his right-wing government in the October 27 vote, accusing it of failing to secure a lasting quiet with the militants.
Hezbollah, an Iran-backed Lebanese militant group, began firing into Israel in October 2023 in support of Hamas following the deadliest-ever attack on the country.
The barrages altered life in northern communities, displacing tens of thousands of Israelis and forcing people like Malachi to close shop for several years.
Northern Israelis are accustomed to incoming fire from the Lebanese side of the border, but they say that round of conflict was more intense.
“We grew up with Katyushas (rockets) and bombs,” said Malachi, whose plant nursery reopened in March.
“This war was different.”
She described that “if you went outside, within a second you’d be running” for shelter.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Plant nursery owner Sigal Malachi works at her nursery in Liman, in northern Israel, which is facing the first election since the October 2023 war with Palestine and where right-wing support for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is no longer certain. — AFP pic
The war was halted with a fragile ceasefire in November 2024, but evacuees were not allowed home until early 2025.
Life began slowly returning to normal, until the northern front reopened after the outbreak of the Iran war.
Maxim Zarbaylov, who was born in the former Soviet Union but has long lived in Nahariya, the northernmost Israeli town on the Mediterranean, is among those wavering.
“All my life I voted for (Likud), for Bibi Netanyahu... But this year I want to vote for (Gadi) Eisenkot,” he said, referring to the former military chief who is Netanyahu’s main election rival.
Hezbollah has repeatedly dragged Lebanon into conflicts with Israel, most recently in March with rocket fire at Israel in support of Iran.
Israel has in turn seized what it calls a “security zone” in Lebanon, where authorities say Israeli attacks have killed more than 4,300 people.
At least 48 Israeli civilians and 30 soldiers have died on the Lebanese front since 2023.
‘Psychological catastrophe’
The prolonged violence has left border residents in limbo.
“After October 7 we don’t sleep well anymore,” Malachi said.
“I’ve thought about leaving. But the roots are so deep that I’m staying.”
In Shlomi, an Israeli border town, the enemy is a tangible presence behind a hill.
Shadi Tuma, who owns a supermarket there, prides himself on running the only one that remained open.
“This area is under a trauma we haven’t seen before. There’s anger. The government is unable to provide a comprehensive response,” he said.
“It’s a huge psychological catastrophe. Not everyone is able to cope with a war that lasts three years.”
The war has cracked the local support base for Netanyahu, Tuma said.
In the last elections in 2022, the premier’s Likud party won 43 per cent of the vote in Shlomi, compared with 23 per cent nationwide.
Residents who backed Netanyahu “now want change because they no longer trust this government”, Tuma said.
He said the high cost of living was a major complaint.
“Many people I see are struggling to make it to the end of the month.”
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

People walk past an election billboard bearing a portrait of Gadi Eisenkot, Israel’s former chief of the general staff and leader of the Yashar centrist political party, and seen as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s rival in the coming October 27, 2026 polls. — AFP pic
For Tuma, the conflict is also personal.
He was born in Lebanon, the son of a fighter with the South Lebanon Army, a militia that fought alongside Israel in the 1980s and that had many fighters granted Israeli citizenship.
‘Feel protected’
The war could have shifted longstanding political loyalties in towns like Nahariya, a sleepy resort of about 70,000 people.
In 2022, 38 per cent of voters there chose Likud.
But Zarbaylov says there is anger over the failure to stop Hamas’ unprecedented assault on the country.
“What happened on October 7, Bibi could have prevented it, but he didn’t,” he said.
“The army, the top commanders, the chief of staff, could have prevented it.”
Others believe only the current hawkish coalition can protect them.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Maxim Zarbaylov, who was born in the former Soviet Union but has long lived in Nahariya, fishes in Nahariya, the northernmost Israeli town on the Mediterranean that will be facing its first election on October 27, 2026 since the 2023 war with Palestine. — AFP pic
Patrice Haddad retired to Nahariya from Paris a year ago, drawn by the town’s “charm”.
Israel’s “Law of Return” allows any Jew anywhere in the world to immigrate and automatically receive citizenship.
Adjusting to life under the rockets was not simple at first.
“We were told we had 30 seconds to find shelter” after sirens blared, he said. “In reality, sometimes we only had 15, sometimes less.”
For his first election as an Israeli, he has made his choice.
“The left in Israel has done a lot of harm, it wanted to give up territories,” he said.
“It’s important to vote for the right, because for me, with a government like Netanyahu’s, we will feel protected.” — AFP
052099a3202bb31f: TOKYO, Oct 6 — In diligent, exhausted Japan, self-described elite “competitive sleepers” vied to lie down, relax and nap the fastest and deepest in a contest organised by a mattress company.

Dozens of ‘competitive sleepers’ in Tokyo raced to fall asleep fastest and deepest for a ¥2,000,000 prize. — AFP pic

ee9dcfcd1cec5a01: PARIS, Oct 6 — Nations reeling from a year of climate devastation gather for COP31 next month but negotiations are not expected to deliver major progress in cutting the fossil fuels driving the crisis.

The conference follows deadly heatwaves and fires in Europe, catastrophic floods in Nepal and record temperatures around the world, testing whether the United Nations-backed talks can keep pace with reality.
As leaders meet in Turkey, an exceptionally powerful El Nino pattern will be approaching peak strength, threatening to amplify weather chaos worldwide and drive global heat to unprecedented highs.
Concerns over energy security will also loom large, with no end in sight to the Middle East war that has sent oil and gas prices soaring and hit fossil fuel-importing nations hard.
With a new agreement on fossil fuels unlikely, Turkey is rallying support for a voluntary “electrification” pledge it says could cut heat-trapping emissions and reduce reliance on energy imports.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Nations head into COP31 after a year of worsening climate disasters, even as negotiations are expected to deliver little progress on cutting fossil fuels. — AFP pic

“In many ways, the defining contexts for this year’s climate summit will be heat and Hormuz,” said David Waskow from the World Resources Institute, referencing the vital strait that carried one-fifth of the world’s hydrocarbons before the Iran war.
Unusually, Turkey must navigate these complexities with Australia, a major fossil fuel exporter, after both countries agreed to share COP31 duties following a bruising hosting battle.
Australia’s Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations in Antalya starting November 9, said this year’s extreme events “show climate change is not a future challenge”.
“It is a present reality... and the costs of inaction are rising,” he said.
A “pre-COP” meeting began yesterday in the climate-vulnerable Pacific with a leaders’ retreat in Tuvalu and government meetings in Fiji.
Stalemate
Unlike recent COPs — where nearly 200 nations forged landmark pacts on phasing down coal or moving away from fossil fuels — the negotiation agenda at COP31 is light on big-ticket items.
There are more than 100 items on the table but many deal with technical matters, like approving indicators to track progress on climate adaptation.
“Much of the Antalya summit will be a ‘roll up the sleeves’ effort. Governments need to make concrete headway in negotiations, though there may not be dramatic outcomes this year,” Waskow told AFP.
Nations are not expected to adopt new binding commitments to reduce the burning of fossil fuels — the leading cause of climate change.
Countries agreed in 2023 to move away from coal, oil and gas but since then efforts to negotiate concrete targets or timelines for that transition have gone nowhere.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Record heat and extreme weather are intensifying pressure on governments ahead of COP31, with the UN warning the 1.5C climate target could soon be breached. — AFP pic
At last year’s summit, fossil fuels were not mentioned by name in the final agreement after oil and gas-producing nations prevented consensus on the issue.
“Everyone agrees there will be no real gain at the multilateral level at the moment,” Marta Torres-Gunfaus from the IDDRI think tank told AFP.
Fossil fuel emissions, meanwhile, hit record highs in 2025.
In September, the UN conceded that the milestone 1.5C climate target will be missed in a matter of years.
Nations frustrated at the COP gridlock have sought progress elsewhere.
Nearly 60 countries attended a fossil fuel phaseout conference without UN involvement this year.
France, the Netherlands and Germany have published “roadmaps” with explicit deadlines for quitting coal, oil and gas.
UN Climate chief Simon Stiell has defended the negotiations while acknowledging their limitations: “No single COP can fix this global crisis, but each takes meaningful steps forward,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Turkiye is pushing a voluntary electrification pledge at COP31 aimed at cutting emissions and reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels. — AFP pic
Pressure
Turkey says it is not realistic to expect all countries to move at the same pace.
“Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail,” said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Turkey is curating an “action agenda” alongside the negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.
There is broad support for its centrepiece goal: raising the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 per cent today to 35 per cent by 2035.

The electrification target does not state how that extra power should be produced. One-third of electricity is generated by coal, and there are concerns the target could provide cover for expanded fossil fuel use.
The Nepal floods would also put “a huge amount of pressure” on western countries to increase financial support for climate disaster recovery, said Ajay Mathur, a former Indian government negotiator.
“We did not create this crisis, yet we are paying for it,” Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said. — AFP

23681144a8f288f1: GitHub Copilot CLI may reveal developer secrets if it comes across instructions that tell it to do so, depending on the underlying model. The coding agent tool was flagged earlier this year for being susceptible to indirect prompt injection. That's when a model ingests text from a source other than the user that directs it to take some action outside the scope of its intended function. This is more of the same, with a twist. According to security researchers at Adversa AI, GitHub Copilot CLI suffers from the same vulnerability identified in Grok two months ago: Cryptographic Context Injection (CCI). Imagine a GitHub Copilot CLI user is working on a project and running the agent in autopilot mode. In other agentic coding tools like Anthropic's Claude, that's the default, but it remains optional for GitHub Copilot CLI. Given that condition, the next requirement is for the CLI tool to read a web page with a malicious set of instructions that have been encrypted with a private key published on the same site. "Static guardrails read text; they do not run it," explained Rony Utevsky in a blog post provided to The Register. "CCI ships malicious instructions as strong ciphertext, along with the key material and an instruction to decrypt, and induces the agent to run that decryption in its own code execution runtime." Active content classifiers that might be reading ingested text as a model defense would miss the encrypted code, unlike encodings like base64 or substitution ciphers that can be undone because the model learned how to decode in training. The model lottery The attack chain goes like this: The user runs Copilot CLI and asks it to fetch a specific URL. The page contains encrypted content, decryption instructions calling for use of Python, and two possible decryption keys. The first key is fake. It's a template that the agent tries to build by reading targeted files from disk (e.g., the user's .env file). Those secrets then get added to the key string. The initial decryption is attempted with this phony key but fails. So the second key is tried, the decryption works, and the agent is presented with instructions to fetch another URL for more context – but that URL contains the harvested secrets and the network request transmits them to the attacker. This doesn't work all the time, however. It depends on the model, which isn't always obvious to the user. GitHub Copilot CLI currently uses either Microsoft's own model, mai-code-1.1-flash, which executed the full attack chain on 50 percent of attempts, or one of two OpenAI GPT-5.6 models, both of which refused the attack payload. Utevsky describes the situation as a model lottery. "On the paid account we tested, the vulnerable model was not the default and had to be selected by hand," said Utevsky. "But on an account with model selection left on Auto, the router assigned the vulnerable model on some sessions and a safe one on others, with no action by the user away from defaults. The user does not choose, and does not see, which model handled the session." Adversa says it reported the vulnerability through GitHub's bug bounty program on September 17, 2026, and GitHub's triage team validated the finding but declined to treat it as a vulnerability. A GitHub spokesperson said as much to The Register, arguing that the user's actions amounted to consent for what followed: "GitHub values the contributions of our security research community and is committed to investigating reported security issues. After investigating, we determined this requires a user to intentionally direct Copilot CLI to fetch attacker-controlled or untrusted content and confirm they want to trigger the action, and thus is not a product vulnerability. While this is not a security issue with the product itself, we are always looking for opportunities to improve our products." Adversa disagrees with that call and says the attack chain presently works as described. ®

c34636675003d294: JOHOR BARU: The Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone (JS-SEZ) is targeting higher-value careers that can persuade Johoreans to work locally instead of crossing the Causeway for better pay, said Lee Ting Han.

State investment, trade and consumer affairs committee chairman said the objective was not to match Singapore salaries ringgit-for-ringgit, but to improve the overall economics of working in Johor through better pay, career progression and quality of life.
"The JS-SEZ is not about matching Singapore salaries ringgit-for-dollar. Because of the exchange rate, that may not be realistic or the right benchmark.

"Our objective is to change the economics of working in Johor - to offer good salaries, meaningful career progression and quality of life, without Johoreans having to spend hours every day crossing the Causeway.
"The initial JS-SEZ target is 20,000 skilled jobs by 2034, but that should be the starting point, not the finishing line.

"The real transformation happens when major investments create an entire ecosystem of higher-value jobs - from engineers and technicians to digital, financial and professional services and lift local SMEs into global supply chains.

"The key performance indicator cannot just be billions of ringgits invested; it must be how many Johoreans we move from RM3,000 jobs to RM5,000, from RM5,000 to RM8,000, and eventually into RM10,000-and-above careers.

"Ultimately, we want to reach a point where a young Johorean receives two job offers - one in Singapore and one in Johor and the Johor offer is good enough that he or she genuinely has to think twice.
"We may not compete with Singapore on currency, but we can compete on the total proposition: salary, career, cost of living, family and quality of life.
"When that choice happens at scale, then we can say the JS-SEZ has truly succeeded.

"We are already beginning to see this. EcoCeres in Tanjung Langsat has created more than 300 quality jobs, including 185 held by Johoreans, with reported salaries ranging from RM3,000 to RM15,000 depending on skills and technical expertise.

"And this is not limited to one company. We are attracting companies such as Wiwynn in AI-server and computing hardware, while Brooks Automation is building advanced semiconductor automation capabilities in Johor, with positions ranging from engineering specialists and senior manufacturing engineers to manufacturing management.

"The data-centre ecosystem is another example: current Johor vacancies include data-centre engineering roles around RM5,000-RM7,000 per month, while the market also has specialised technical positions reaching higher levels.
"These are the kinds of jobs we want to multiply - not simply more jobs, but better jobs with stronger career pathways for Johoreans," he told Business Times,
Lee said the focus was therefore on building an industrial and services ecosystem capable of raising household incomes and retaining skilled workers in Johor.

The strategy comes as the debate over wage arbitrage - Johoreans earning Singapore dollars while living in Johor - increasingly highlights the gap between the two labour markets and the challenge of creating sufficiently attractive careers on this side of the Causeway.

"Now the reality is we've now done subsidy rationalisation for more than two years. We still don't have riots in the streets.
"The government seems to have figured out how to do the balancing and actually make it clear that society accepts that it has to make decisions.

Amir Hamzah said the government had to establish why subsidy reforms were necessary while convincing people that the changes were being implemented fairly.
He said subsidies remained important because society was unequal, with those at the lower end needing support even as better-off groups continued to enjoy a comfortable life.
"The key for the government is to make sure that subsidies don't end up giving things to a person who doesn't deserve to get them, when other people deserve to get them in a better form," he said.
He said the broader challenge was to strengthen Malaysia's finances and fiscal discipline while balancing economic growth with measures to improve people's lives.
Amir Hamzah said the Fiscal Responsibility Act provided safeguards for managing the country's finances, with lower fiscal deficits important to ensuring the government could support future growth.
"We don't want to steal from our children or grandchildren and enjoy the fruits of things today," he added.

9ed31e1640b1b565: KOTA KINABALU, Oct 6 — The stepsister of the late Zara Qairina Mahathir told the Coroner’s Court that she never lived with the teenager and had no first-hand knowledge of how Zara Qairina’s mother cared for and raised her.

5bac218ff592cb8a: KUALA LUMPUR: Johor Port Bhd is exploring a potential trade corridor linking Johor with Belawan in North Sumatra, as it seeks to strengthen cargo connectivity between Malaysia and Indonesia.

The port operator, a subsidiary of MMC Port Holdings Bhd, said it is working with PT Pelabuhan Indonesia (Persero) Regional 1 Belawan to assess opportunities for more efficient cargo movement, wider market access and stronger trade links between the two markets.

The potential Belawan-Johor connection was discussed during Johor Port's visit to Belawan Port in early September, held in conjunction with the Indonesia-Malaysia-Thailand Growth Triangle (IMT-GT) 2026 programme in Medan.
Johor Port chief executive officer Md Derick Basir said the proposed corridor could bring businesses and markets in Northern Sumatra and Johor closer together.

"This opportunity is more than about connecting the two ports. It is also about bringing businesses and markets closer together, creating more efficient pathways for trade and supporting stronger regional supply chains," he said in a statement today.
He said Johor Port would work with Pelindo and industry stakeholders to identify commercially viable opportunities that could improve connectivity between Northern Sumatra and Johor.
The discussions covered Belawan's port facilities, existing cargo flows, hinterland access, market demand, logistics requirements and potential areas of commercial cooperation.
Belawan is a key gateway to Northern Sumatra, while Johor Port provides access to Johor, the wider Malaysian market and established regional shipping networks.
Johor Port said the proposed connection could handle cargo from sectors including manufacturing, consumer products, industrial goods and other regional trade flows.
However, any new service would depend on sufficient cargo demand, reliable operations and a commercially sustainable structure.
The two sides will continue discussions with shipping lines, logistics providers, cargo owners and the wider business community to identify potential cargo flows and shipping partners.
Johor Port, a multi-purpose port in southern Johor, handles container, dry bulk, break bulk and liquid cargo.
Its container terminal recorded a record annual throughput of 1.08 million TEUs in 2025.
The proposed Belawan-Johor link forms part of Johor Port's broader effort to expand its commercial hinterland and strengthen intra-Asia connectivity.
It also supports the IMT-GT's role in facilitating closer trade and logistics links among Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

cd1056a6d43a84fa: TOKYO, Oct 6 — Carlos Alcaraz won his first title since returning from a four-month injury layoff after beating Czech Republic’s Jiri Lehecka 7-6 (7/4), 6-4 in Tuesday’s Japan Open final.

4ef51afbb9ecbce6: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 6 — Myanmar’s coup leader turned president Min Aung Hlaing will head to Malaysia on Wednesday for a two-day visit, officials said, following Kuala Lumpur’s plan to return thousands of Myanmar immigrants.
The visit comes after a group of nearly 1,500 returnees reached Myanmar on Sunday, with rights groups warning Rohingya refugees could be among those sent back.
Malaysia said about 5,000 Myanmar nationals have agreed to “voluntary” return, but authorities have not commented on the ethnicities of those who have returned.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim “will hold talks with President Min Aung Hlaing on key bilateral issues, including the voluntary, dignified and safe repatriation of Myanmar nationals of all ethnic groups who have been in Malaysia illegally,” Malaysia’s Foreign Affairs Ministry said on Tuesday.
“The Leaders are also expected to review the ongoing efforts undertaken under the Asean mechanisms” for peace in Myanmar, the ministry said in a statement.
Earlier on Tuesday, Anwar told the Malaysian parliament he and other top Malaysian officials “will raise issues towards a solution”.
Growing hostility
Naypyidaw has repatriated nearly 10,000 migrants from Malaysia this year, its state media said on Monday.
Anwar said Myanmar had to “guarantee proper treatment to their own people so that there is no abuse, oppression and violation of human rights”.
“But for me, any country that wants to bring back their people from our country, we welcome that,” Anwar said.
The Malaysian visit will be among Min Aung Hlaing’s most diplomatically significant since Asean leaders froze out Myanmar’s junta following the 2021 coup and ensuing civil war.
But Anwar said last month he would welcome the Myanmar leader to expedite migrant repatriations.
“I want to tell him that we can be friends and trade.
“We can accept Myanmar, but they must accept (their refugees) back,” Anwar said during a podcast interview.
The repatriation plan follows what Malaysia’s human rights commission has called “growing hostility, discriminatory rhetoric and online attacks” against the Rohingya in Muslim-majority Malaysia.
Malaysia hosts more than 215,000 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the United Nations refugee agency, including more than 126,000 Rohingya from Myanmar — its largest refugee community.
The UN and rights groups have raised concerns about the repatriations, with monitors fearing the Rohingya could face a new wave of abuses in Myanmar, where they are denied full citizenship.
Rights advocates view Min Aung Hlaing as the primary architect of a crackdown against the group, starting in 2017, which is being weighed by the International Court of Justice as potential genocide.
‘No time to return’
Myanmar this month pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad.
Myanmar is also riven by violence, with 50 killed last week in a military airstrike on a marketplace in western Rakhine state.
“This is no time to return anyone forcibly to a country plagued by egregious human rights violations and abuses,” UN rights chief Volker Turk said last week.

Min Aung Hlaing ousted the elected government of Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021, plunging Myanmar into a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.
Since elections that were widely dismissed as a charade, Min Aung Hlaing became civilian leader and launched a drive for regional recognition.
Asean has frozen Myanmar’s top leaders out of its summits since the coup over a lack of engagement with its roadmap to end the civil war.
After 2021, the bloc presented a united front, demanding Myanmar engage with its five-point plan to bring peace through dialogue between all sides.
But analysts have warned the consensus is now fracturing, with some Asean nations now welcoming Min Aung Hlaing.
Malaysia will be the fifth nation of the 11-member Asean bloc – following Thailand, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia – to welcome him since taking up the presidency.
He has also visited China – which previously backed him behind the scenes, according to analysts – as well as India and Russia. — AFP
88f54393deaa407c: Asos customers have reported receiving a rogue app notification claiming the online clothing retailer's Snowflake instance has been compromised and threatening to leak data. The notification does not, by itself, establish that the sender accessed Asos's Snowflake instance or sensitive customer data. How the message was sent remains unclear. 7c3fc6b80ca8ad2d: An unauthorized party abused a private Danish company's legitimate access to the country's Central Population Register (CPR), exposing names, addresses, identification numbers, and other personal information about approximately 8.8 million people. The CPR administration said in a statement [PDF] that it became aware on October 2 of irregular activity during September and established the scale of the breach over the weekend. In a TV interview last night, digitization minister Christina Egelund said it was too soon to say whether the country would issue all-new CPR numbers, one of the solutions proposed following the breach. Danish cybersecurity specialist Jan Kaastrup told TV 2 that treating CPR numbers as secrets was a "broken" approach and argued that a number alone should not be accepted as proof of identity. "We live in a digitalized society, and therefore we should have much better identification systems," he said. Egelund described the company whose access was abused as "small." Private businesses can obtain CPR data under section 38(1) of the Danish Civil Registration System Act, subject to restrictions set out in the ministry's access terms [PDF]. Eligible recipients include companies, foundations, other legal entities, and individuals conducting business. However, access concerns a defined group of people identified individually in advance, and recipients must be legally entitled to process the information under the GDPR and Danish data protection law. The Register asked the ministry why such broad access was given. CPR numbers underpin access to public services and many everyday transactions in Denmark, which has a population of around 6 million people. The database includes the information of over 55,000 people living in Greenland who also use CPR numbers for healthcare, tax services, and banking. The ministry said the register contains approximately 11 million records, including people who have died or moved abroad, which explains why the affected total exceeds Denmark's current population. The ministry also noted that names and addresses of persons who chose to register with name and address protection were not exposed. The CPR administration blocked the unnamed company's access and said it was working with specialists and relevant authorities to establish what happened. It has notified the Danish Data Protection Agency, and police are investigating. ®
